Frequently Asked Questions

Where can I review the stories published about West Virginia’s settlement spending?

These stories were published by 100 Days in Appalachia as part of the Price of Recovery series.

What counts as a public record?

Generally, records created or maintained by government agencies while conducting official business are considered public records. This may include emails, financial records, meeting minutes, and contracts.

How long does it take to receive records?

Response timelines vary by state. Some agencies respond within a few days, while others may take weeks or months, depending on the request scope.

What if agencies don’t have organized records?

In some cases, agencies may not maintain clear documentation of spending decisions. This itself may become a reporting finding, highlighting gaps in transparency or recordkeeping.

What if my request is denied?

If an agency denies your request, ask them to cite the specific legal exemption being used. You may be able to:

  • Narrow the request
  • Request partially redacted documents
  • File an appeal under your state’s open records law

What if the municipality or county says they haven’t spent any of the money?

Then you have a great story. As of March 2026, we are nearly four years into the process of distributing funds. What is keeping the entity from spending them? Is it a lack of knowledge of what to spend it on? Guidance from a state or federal agency? A lack of local resources to plan for spending?

The opportunity is ripe for finding out why they haven’t spent any funds, then asking experts in your community — both medical/academic and people with lived experience — how they should spend it.

My state has funding and a separate process for distributing the funds. What’s the difference between that and the county/municipality?

The difference is solely who holds the money and who gets to spend it. Many states, like West Virginia, created state-level nonprofits to distribute state-level funds or gave the responsibility to a specific state entity (like a department, agency, or office).

Those funds come from the same sources, but typically state entities have more resources to determine where, how, and how much to spend. Many municipalities and counties — particularly in rural parts of the country — do not have the same bureaucratic infrastructure. That’s why coverage of local funds is:

  1. Critical — the decisions are happening with little public scrutiny
  2. Ripe for deep-dive data reporting — the records are public, the amounts are significant, and the accountability gap is wide

Can I review the West Virginia documents?

Yes. All documents from the investigation are available on DocumentCloud. You can find them by searching “West Virginia Opioid Settlement Spending” or visiting the DocumentCloud project page.

I’m a journalism instructor or student newsroom leader who would like to replicate this process. Do you have help for me?

Yes. We are turning all of our work into a curriculum for college classrooms. It will be fully complete by May 2026, but there are materials available now to begin planning.
